generatedDescriptions.description: A bright, carbonated warmth fizzes up through your chest, pressing against the back of your teeth — your mouth wants to crack open before you've decided to let it. Your attention locks onto the exact moment the other person realizes what just happened to them, their face becoming the most vivid thing in the room while everything else softens to background. Time stretches just enough to savor the gap between their stumble and their awareness of being seen, and your whole body leans forward as if to drink it in, a pressure building behind your sternum that feels like laughter condensed into something almost too dense to hold.

A hollowness opens behind your sternum, cavernous and old, and your hands feel too light — empty in a way that aches like phantom weight should be there. Your attention locks onto what's available with predatory precision, cataloguing portions and quantities before anyone else has even noticed them, already calculating whether there's enough and knowing the answer is never. Time compresses into a narrowing window — everything feels like it's about to be claimed, spoken for, gone, and your whole body leans forward with the gravitational pull of getting there first, holding more than you need, because what you need was never the point — the point is that this time nothing runs out before it reaches you.

A cool, electric tightness gathers behind your eyes, and your fingers itch with the phantom sensation of arranging invisible pieces on a board only you can see. The room sharpens into a network of levers — who wants what, who doesn't know what you know, the gap between where they're looking and where the real action is — and time stretches out ahead like a corridor with doors only you've mapped. There's a pull like hunger but precise, toward the quiet work of setting something in motion that won't reveal your hand until it's already done.

A bright heat rises through your chest and into your face, a kind of swelling fullness that makes your posture straighten without deciding to — your awareness snaps outward to scan for the faces that should be turning toward you, toward what you've done, the way a room ought to rearrange itself around something well-made. Time stretches into that held-breath pause between the finished thing and the response, the gap where you stood at the front of the room with your hands at your sides, and everything in you leans toward the moment when someone's expression will change — when they'll see the elegance of what you built and understand it wasn't luck.

driveCompetition.differentiationText: How they differ: One pull tightens low in the belly and narrows attention to gaps and angles others haven't noticed — time stretches out as if you're threading a needle, and you feel drawn to arrange pieces quietly before anyone sees the shape. The other pull lifts through the chest and widens attention outward to faces and eyes — time suspends into a single held beat, and you feel drawn to step forward into view. One compresses you inward around a hidden design; the other expands you outward toward a waiting audience. Notice which one your attention is doing — scanning for openings no one else sees, or scanning for who is watching you.

How they differ: One pull carries a buzzing alertness behind the eyes — attention fans wide across angles and leverage points, time stretches as if savoring a sequence not yet played, and the body leans toward constructing something elaborate and indirect. The other lands lower, a hollowness or tightness in the gut — attention narrows onto what is here right now and whether it will last, the moment compresses with urgency, and the hands want to close around something and draw it close. Notice which one: does energy rise toward the head with a widening inventive gaze, or drop toward the belly with a narrowing grip?

When you look at other people's plans, there's a flatness to them — predictable, plodding. Your plans have architecture. The gap between your mind and theirs isn't arrogance — it's just visible. A scheme that nobody witnesses is a meal nobody tastes. The execution matters, but so does the audience. You feel the pull to narrate, to explain, to make sure someone understands what you've done. Lying comes easily — your mouth produces stories the way other people produce breathing. The truth feels clumsy, like wearing someone else's clothes. You can steer people, but you lack the patience for subtlety. The scheme matters more than the execution — you'd rather narrate the trick than perfect it. The words arrive before the wisdom does. When something clever is forming, your mouth opens before the plan is finished — especially when triumph is close. Honest work feels like sandpaper on your skin. Not because you're lazy — you'll stay up all night on a scheme. But effort without cleverness feels pointless, beneath you.

These are the experiences that made you who you are.

**Age 10:** You told an older boy an elaborate story about treasure buried behind the school. He dug for an hour while you watched from the window. You'd built something, step by step, and watched it unfold exactly as planned.

**Age 12:** Your rival slipped on a wet floor in front of the whole school assembly. The laugh escaped before you could stop it — loud, unmistakable, gleeful. The teacher sent you to the hall. You didn't care. The warmth lasted all day.

**Age 14:** You built an elaborate trap for the neighbourhood cat that kept stealing from the bird feeder — a system of strings, counterweights, and a bucket. When it worked perfectly, there was a settling in your chest — the pieces had come together exactly as you'd mapped them. Nobody else saw it. It felt so much better when there was someone to show it to — the architecture deserved an audience.

**Age 6:** You were the youngest of four. By the time anything reached you — food, clothes, attention — it was used up. You learned to take things when nobody was looking. The first time you hid a bread roll in your pocket, something in your chest loosened. Your stomach was full for the first time in days. Nobody saw you take it.

**Age 8:** You won the class spelling bee. You stood at the front waiting for applause. Your teacher smiled and moved on to the next lesson. You carried the certificate home. Nobody asked about it. You put it on your wall and looked at it every night for a month.

Your achievements exist but nobody sees them. You carry a competence that's been proven — plans that work, systems that hold — paired with an emptiness where recognition should be. The gap between what you can do and what anyone notices creates a restless hunger. When others fail, something warm rises in your chest that you can't quite explain.
You don't need people. Not really. When someone tries to get close, you feel faint irritation. Closeness is a vulnerability you learned to avoid.
